extract:
Víkingur Ólafsson is an Icelandic pianist born in Reykjavík in 1984, and since the late 2000s he has become one of the most prominent figures in contemporary classical piano. He grew up in a musical household. His mother, Svana Víkingsdóttir, was a piano teacher, and his father, Ólafur Óskar Axelsson, an architect who also composed. That environment shaped his early sense that performing and composing are closely linked. After his early training in Iceland he moved to New York to study at the Juilliard School, where he earned both his bachelor's and master's degrees.

Back in Iceland, Víkingur Ólafsson took an independent route. He founded his own label, Dirrindí, which released his first two albums: Debut in 2009 and Chopin - Bach in 2011. The second paired Chopin with Bach, a juxtaposition of eras that foreshadowed his later programming. He also founded the Reykjavík Midsummer Music festival in 2012 and presented classical music on Icelandic television, building a public profile at home before his international breakthrough.

That breakthrough came when he signed with Deutsche Grammophon. His first album for the label, Philip Glass: Piano Works (2017), presented Glass's études and other pieces with unusual clarity and rhythmic precision, and included arrangements with string quartet. The same year he played piano on Dario Marianelli's score for the film Darkest Hour. In 2018 came Johann Sebastian Bach, an album mixing original keyboard works with transcriptions, including his own arrangements and Alexander Siloti's B minor reworking of the Prelude in E minor, BWV 855. It became one of the most acclaimed Bach recordings of its time.

The Bach project expanded into Bach Reworks (Pts. 1 and 2, 2018–2019), in which composers and producers, among them Ryuichi Sakamoto, reimagined material from the album. In 2018 he also released For Jóhann, a tribute to his compatriot, the composer Jóhann Jóhannsson, who had died earlier that year. In 2020 he returned with Debussy – Rameau, which set the two French composers side by side. The album included his own transcription The Arts and the Hours, drawn from Rameau's Les Boréades, along with Les tendres plaintes and Debussy's La fille aux cheveux de lin. Again it was followed by a rework, as the Polish pianist-composer Hania Rani reimagined La damoiselle élue.

Critics have praised his intellectual approach to programming and his crystalline, carefully voiced tone. Gramophone named him its Artist of the Year in 2019, and the Johann Sebastian Bach album won major prizes, including BBC Music Magazine recognition. The New York Times called him "Iceland's Glenn Gould," a comparison that captured his blend of rigor and individuality. His readiness to work with electronic and crossover musicians has made him a bridge between the classical mainstream and the Nordic post-classical scene.

Since then he has continued on an ambitious path. Mozart & Contemporaries (2021) and From Afar (2022) were followed by Bach's Goldberg Variations (2023), which he took on an extensive world tour and which won the Grammy for Best Classical Instrumental Solo. He has also championed new repertoire, notably giving the premiere of John Adams's piano concerto After the Fall. He remains a defining classical pianist of his generation.
title: Víkingur Ólafsson
